angularDiameterSource: The 59.8 +/- 0.4 mas stellar disc Vlemmings et al. (2024, Nature 633, 323) fit to the ALMA 338 GHz visibilities, with an axis ratio of 0.99 +/- 0.01. Measured again here on the archive image this package ships: the half-power diameter is 60 mas. The near-infrared photosphere is smaller, 51.18 +/- 2.24 mas (Ohnaka et al. 2019, ApJ 883, 89), because 338 GHz sees a layer above it, and the 1.25 micrometre uniform disc is 57 +/- 5 mas (Bedding et al. 1997, MNRAS 286, 957), the largest stellar diameter in the JMMC JMDC.
distanceSource: Hipparcos parallax 18.31 +/- 0.99 mas (van Leeuwen 2007) via SIMBAD: 54.615 pc. Vlemmings et al. (2024, Nature 633, 323) adopt the same measurement as 55 +/- 3 pc and state that there is no useable Gaia parallax for this star.
radiusSource: The 59.8 +/- 0.4 mas disc above, at the 54.615 pc Hipparcos distance: 351 solar radii at 695700 km per solar radius, against the 353 +/- 19 Vlemmings et al. (2024) give at their rounded 55 pc. The same ALMA image is this object's lens, so the sphere and its texture are the same star.
effectiveTemperatureSource: Effective temperature 2710 ± 70 K from Ohnaka, Weigelt & Hofmann 2019 (ApJ 883, 89; https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ab3d2a), Table 1 and Section 3: the AMBER limb-darkened diameter 51.18 mas with the bolometric flux compiled over several epochs. The radius source, Vlemmings et al. 2024, adopts this value.

shape.qualification: A sphere at the published radius. The photosphere of an asymptotic giant branch star is not a solid surface and its limb is not sharp; the sphere is the reference surface the ALMA image is cast onto, not a measured shape. Its 338 GHz disc is 1.18 +/- 0.11 times the infrared photosphere.
